warmup.q: In which JDK can you compile value record Shelf(short floor, short row) {} today?
options: JDK 21: records are value types already, so value is just allowed
JDK 27, where value classes became final
Only early-access builds of JDK 28, with --enable-preview
warmup.why: JEP 401 (value objects, preview) was integrated into the JDK's main code line after JDK 27 had branched off, so it arrives in JDK 28, scheduled for March 2027; early-access builds have it now. JDK 25, 26 and 27 don't. Records are identity objects on every released JDK: == compares references, and you can synchronize on them. The last section covers it.

opening:
When a member reserves a book this library doesn't own, the request goes to the regional catalogue, a program run by another organization that knows what every library nearby holds. Its answer comes back as text fields: a status, and a few boxes that should be filled in only for some statuses. A ready book has a pickup code and a hold shelf. An unavailable one has a reason. A waiting-list place has an expected wait.

Picture it as one paper form with every box printed on it. Nothing stops someone from ticking Ready and also writing "Reason: lost". The form allows 48 combinations, and 3 of them make sense. The easy trap is to trust the notes beside the boxes, not the shape of the form.

The last three lessons gave us records, sealed types and a clerk who sorts by shape. In this lesson, we'll put them together: forms that can't be filled in wrong, one door where outside answers are checked, and the rules kept in one place. Then we'll look at Project Valhalla, which wants to print small forms straight onto the page. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with one form for the catalogue's answer and 48 ways to fill it in. Three records under a sealed interface left only the 3 that make sense, one clerk at the door checked everything from outside, and the rules moved into functions with one switch each. Valhalla may one day print small forms straight onto the page, but today a record is still a form in its own envelope.

Now look in your own code for a class with a status field and several nullable fields beside it. Count its shapes.

That ends this track. Next, we'll start Advanced Kotlin with inline functions. What happens when the compiler pastes a function and its lambda straight into the caller?

sections.html:
Here is how the catalogue's answer usually arrives in a program: one class, every field optional.

Java
public class HoldReplyDto {
    String status;               // "READY", "UNAVAILABLE" or "WAITLISTED"
    String pickupCode;           // only when ready
    Integer holdShelf;           // only when ready
    String reasonCode;           // only when unavailable
    Integer waitDays;            // only when waitlisted
}
Kotlin
data class HoldReplyDto(
    val status: String?,         // "READY", "UNAVAILABLE" or "WAITLISTED"
    val pickupCode: String?,     // only when ready
    val holdShelf: Int?,         // only when ready
    val reasonCode: String?,     // only when unavailable
    val waitDays: Int?,          // only when waitlisted
)

A DTO, short for data transfer object, is a class whose only job is to hold the fields of a message as they arrived. Count what this one allows. Three statuses, times four optional fields that are each set or null, gives 48 shapes. Three of them make sense. The other 45, such as ready with no pickup code, or ready with a reason code, can be built, stored and passed around. The comments are the only place that says which fields go together. Every piece of code that reads the DTO has to check that again, and one of them won't. The IllegalStates demo hands a broken reply to the code that prints pickup slips:

shapes the DTO allows: 48, shapes that make sense: 3
DTO consumer:    print slip: shelf 12, code null

A member now holds a slip with no code on it, and the desk can't hand over the book. Model the three outcomes instead, each with only its own fields:

Java
public sealed interface HoldResult permits Ready, Unavailable, Waitlisted {}
public record Ready(PickupCode code, int shelf) implements HoldResult {}
public record Unavailable(Reason reason) implements HoldResult {}
public record Waitlisted(Duration expectedWait) implements HoldResult {}
Kotlin
sealed interface HoldResult {
    data class Ready(val code: PickupCode, val shelf: Int) : HoldResult
    data class Unavailable(val reason: Reason) : HoldResult
    data class Waitlisted(val expectedWait: Duration) : HoldResult
}

Now there are three shapes, and "ready with a reason" can't even be written down. In the paperwork picture, the one form with every box has become three forms, each with only its own boxes. The checks that are left move into the constructors: a pickup code is six letters or digits, and hold shelves start at 1. (The component is expectedWait, not wait; lesson 1's aside showed why Java refuses that name.)

That's what "make illegal states unrepresentable" means in practice: the types and the canonical constructors refuse the bad values once, so no reader has to. Brian Goetz calls this style data-oriented programming: model the data as immutable records and sealed types, and write the logic as functions over them. He wrote it up in a 2022 InfoQ article, "Data Oriented Programming in Java".

His 2019 design note on records and sealed types gives the vocabulary. A record is a product type: a Ready is a code and a shelf, and its API models "the state, the whole state, and nothing but the state". A sealed interface is a sum type, "a discriminated union of a fixed set of types": a HoldResult is ready or unavailable or waitlisted. Most messages a program handles have exactly this shape, a few alternatives, each a fixed set of fields.

A shape that can't be built can't be mishandled. Give each valid combination its own record.

Three clean forms help only if every answer from outside is copied onto one of them. That copying needs a place.

try.title: Count the shapes, then build a bad one
steps: Run IllegalStates (or IllegalStatesKt). Read the DTO consumer line: what will the member find on the slip?
In the Java demo, try to build a Ready with a reason code. There is no constructor for it: the shape doesn't exist.
In the Kotlin twin, change HoldResult.Ready("", 12) to HoldResult.Ready(null, 12) and run. Which tool stopped you this time?

code.title: IllegalStates.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l04.demo; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.Objects; /** One class with optional fields, against a sealed model that has only the valid shapes. */ public class IllegalStates { // the "bag of optionals" a JSON mapper gives you for the catalogue's reply to a hold request static final class HoldReplyDto { final String status; // "READY", "UNAVAILABLE" or "WAITLISTED" final String pickupCode; // should be set only when ready final String reasonCode; // should be set only when unavailable final Integer waitDays; // should be set only when waitlisted final Integer holdShelf; // should be set only when ready HoldReplyDto(String status, String pickupCode, String reasonCode, Integer waitDays, Integer holdShelf) { this.status = status; this.pickupCode = pickupCode; this.reasonCode = reasonCode; this.waitDays = waitDays; this.holdShelf = holdShelf; } } // a consumer of the DTO: it trusts that the fields match the status static String pickupSlip(HoldReplyDto r) { if ("READY".equals(r.status)) return "print slip: shelf " + r.holdShelf + ", code " + r.pickupCode; return "no slip"; } // the same information as a closed model: three shapes, each with only its own fields sealed interface HoldResult permits Ready, Unavailable, Waitlisted {} record Ready(String pickupCode, int shelf) implements HoldResult { Ready { Objects.requireNonNull(pickupCode, "pickupCode"); if (shelf < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("hold shelves start at 1"); } } record Unavailable(String reasonCode) implements HoldResult {} record Waitlisted(Duration expectedWait) implements HoldResult {} static String pickupSlip(HoldResult r) { return switch (r) { case Ready(var code, var shelf) -> "print slip: shelf " + shelf + ", code " + code; case Unavailable u -> "no slip"; case Waitlisted w -> "no slip yet"; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { int statuses = 3, optionalFields = 4; System.out.println("shapes the DTO allows: " + statuses * (1 << optionalFields) + ", shapes that make sense: 3"); // ready, but with no pickup code and a reason code: nothing stops it HoldReplyDto broken = new HoldReplyDto("READY", null, "10", null, 12); System.out.println("DTO consumer: " + pickupSlip(broken)); try { new Ready(null, 12); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("sealed model: refused, " + e.getMessage() + " is required"); } System.out.println("sealed consumer: " + pickupSlip(new Ready("K7P2QX", 12))); } }

init { require(pickupCode.isNotBlank()) { "pickupCode is required" } require(shelf >= 1) { "hold shelves start at 1" } } } data class Unavailable(val reasonCode: String?) : HoldResult data class Waitlisted(val expectedWait: Duration) : HoldResult } fun pickupSlip(r: HoldResult): String = when (r) { is HoldResult.Ready -> "print slip: shelf ${r.shelf}, code ${r.pickupCode}" is HoldResult.Unavailable -> "no slip" is HoldResult.Waitlisted -> "no slip yet" } /** One class with optional fields, against a sealed model that has only the valid shapes. */ fun main() { val statuses = 3 val optionalFields = 4 println("shapes the DTO allows: ${statuses * (1 shl optionalFields)}, shapes that make sense: 3") // ready, but with no pickup code and a reason code: nothing stops it val broken = HoldReplyDto("READY", null, "10", null, 12) println("DTO consumer: ${pickupSlip(broken)}") // HoldResult.Ready(null, 12) doesn't even compile: the type says the code is there try { HoldResult.Ready("", 12) } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println("sealed model: refused, ${e.message}") } println("sealed consumer: ${pickupSlip(HoldResult.Ready("K7P2QX", 12))}") }

try.expect: Both print shapes the DTO allows: 48, shapes that make sense: 3, then DTO consumer: print slip: shelf 12, code null: nothing stopped a ready reply with no code. The sealed model refuses it (pickupCode is required), and the valid hold prints print slip: shelf 12, code K7P2QX. In Kotlin, Ready(null, 12) doesn't compile at all, because the property is a non-null String: the type system did the constructor's job.

sections.h: Parse at the edge, then trust the types
sections.html:
The sealed model helps only if untrusted data can't get in around it. So the program turns raw input into the model in exactly one place, at its edge: the code that reads the catalogue's message. Everything behind the edge works only with model values. In the picture, letters from outside arrive in any handwriting. One clerk at the door copies each onto the right form, or sends it back with a polite note saying what was wrong.

Java
static Parsed parse(HoldReplyDto raw) {
    try {
        return switch (raw.status) {
            case "READY" -> raw.pickupCode == null || raw.holdShelf == null
                    ? new Rejected("ready without a code or a shelf")
                    : new Ok(new Ready(new PickupCode(raw.pickupCode), raw.holdShelf));
            case "UNAVAILABLE" -> new Ok(new Unavailable(Reason.fromCode(raw.reasonCode)));
            case "WAITLISTED" -> raw.waitDays == null
                    ? new Rejected("waiting list without a wait")
                    : new Ok(new Waitlisted(Duration.ofDays(raw.waitDays)));
            case null, default -> new Rejected("unknown status: " + raw.status);
        };
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
        return new Rejected(e.getMessage());          // a constructor refused a value
    }
}
Kotlin
fun parse(raw: HoldReplyDto): Parsed = try {
    when (raw.status) {
        "READY" ->
            if (raw.pickupCode == null || raw.holdShelf == null) Rejected("ready without a code or a shelf")
            else Ok(Ready(PickupCode(raw.pickupCode), raw.holdShelf))
        "UNAVAILABLE" -> Ok(Unavailable(Reason.fromCode(raw.reasonCode)))
        "WAITLISTED" ->
            if (raw.waitDays == null) Rejected("waiting list without a wait")
            else Ok(Waitlisted(Duration.ofDays(raw.waitDays.toLong())))
        else -> Rejected("unknown status: ${raw.status}")
    }
} catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) {
    Rejected(e.message ?: "invalid reply")            // a constructor refused a value
}

Read parse from the top. It switches on the status string. A ready reply needs its code and its shelf, or it's rejected with a reason. An unavailable reply looks up its code in a small table of reasons. A waiting-list reply needs its days. Anything else, null included, is rejected. The tricky part is the try around it all: it catches the IllegalArgumentException a constructor throws when it refuses a value, and turns it into a Rejected too.

Two details make this work. The function never throws. A reply the model refuses comes back as Rejected with a reason. The caller decides what that means (log it, ask the catalogue again, tell the member to ask at the desk), and no exception escapes from somewhere deep inside. And the constructors stay the final check: parse doesn't repeat the pickup-code rule, it calls new PickupCode(...) and reports the refusal.

Behind the edge, nothing checks again. A method that takes a Ready knows it has a valid code and a real shelf, because no other kind of Ready can exist. Records and sealed types make this cheap: the model is a dozen lines, the edge is one function, and the compiler checks every switch in between. The lab builds exactly this, in Kotlin, including a case the snippets above skip: a ready reply that also carries a reason code contradicts itself, and must be rejected.

Check outside data once, at the door. Behind the door, trust the types.

Only good forms get in now. The next question is where the rules that read them should live.

try.title: Predict what the door does
steps: The catalogue sends status: "READY " (with a trailing space), pickup code K7P2QX and hold shelf 12. Which arm of parse takes it, and what does the pickup desk see?
It sends a waiting-list reply with waitDays: 0. Does parse or a constructor produce the result?
A teammate adds if (ready.shelf() < 1) return; inside the code that prints slips. Can that line ever run?
try.expect: The trailing space matches no status string, so case null, default returns Rejected("unknown status: READY "), and the pickup desk never sees the reply: a strict door turns a sloppy reply into a visible rejection instead of a slip with bad data. The zero wait gets past parse, because the field isn't null, and is refused by the Waitlisted constructor once it has the range check (as the lab's does); the catch turns that refusal into Rejected. The teammate's line is dead code: a Ready with a shelf below 1 can't be built, so the check can never be true.

sections.h: Keep the rules in one place: operations live outside the data
sections.html:
In classic object-oriented design, behavior lives in the classes: result.screenMessage(), result.nextStep(), result.reminderText(), each written three times, across Ready, Unavailable and Waitlisted. Data-oriented code keeps the records plain and writes each operation as one function with a switch. In the picture, the forms stay plain, and the rules live in one binder at the desk:

Java
static String screenMessage(HoldResult r) {
    return switch (r) {
        case Ready(var code, var shelf) -> "Your book is waiting on hold shelf " + shelf + ".";
        case Unavailable(var reason) when reason == Reason.ACCOUNT_BLOCKED -> "Please ask at the desk.";
        case Unavailable u -> "This title is not available right now.";
        case Waitlisted(var wait) -> "You're on the waiting list. Expected wait: " + wait.toDays() + " days.";
    };
}
Kotlin
fun screenMessage(r: HoldResult): String = when (r) {
    is Ready -> "Your book is waiting on hold shelf ${r.shelf}."
    is Unavailable if r.reason == Reason.ACCOUNT_BLOCKED -> "Please ask at the desk."
    is Unavailable -> "This title is not available right now."
    is Waitlisted -> "You're on the waiting list. Expected wait: ${r.expectedWait.toDays()} days."
}

Everything about the screen at the self-service desk sits in one function. The records don't depend on screen text, and the next operation, say the text message sent to the member's phone, is a new function that touches nothing else. Note the account-blocked line: the screen stands in a public place, so it never says what's wrong with an account.

That's one side of the expression problem, which Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento in the patterns track introduced. It says that no design makes both kinds of change cheap: adding a new type, and adding a new operation. With methods on the classes, adding a type is local, and adding an operation means editing every class. With sealed types and switches it's the other way round: a new operation is one function, and a new type breaks every switch until you handle it. The figure shows the grid. Choose by the change you expect more often.

For the library's data (hold results, desk events, loans, copy statuses) the set of types changes rarely, and new operations keep arriving: a new report, a new reminder, a new screen. So the data-oriented side wins there. For open hierarchies that others extend, such as the partner libraries' PartnerItem from lesson 2, keep an interface with methods. And behavior that's about the value itself, like Shelfmark.next(), belongs on the record. Keep the library's rules out of the records; small methods that compute with the value itself can stay.

The ExpressionProblem demo lets you pay both costs. Its Activity records what happened on a member's account, a book borrowed, returned or renewed, and two functions switch over it:

borrowed Dune for 21 days
borrowed Emma for 21 days
returned Dune
renewed  Emma for 14 more days
books out: 1

Adding a third function changes no existing line. Adding a Lost activity breaks both switches, and the compiler lists each one.

Plain data, rules in functions. A new rule then touches one place, and a new type is found by the compiler.

Records and sealed types settle how the data is shaped. How the JVM stores that data is the last part of the story.

try.title: Pay both costs
steps: Write operation 3 where the comment says: sendsReceipt, true for borrowing and renewing (the member gets the new due date), false for returns. How many existing lines did you change?
Add the Lost record (in Java, add it to permits too) and run. List the places the compiler asks you to change.

code.title: ExpressionProblem.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l04.demo; import java.util.List; /** Data in records, operations in functions. Add an operation, then add a type, and compare the cost. */ public class ExpressionProblem { // what can happen on a member's account sealed interface Activity permits Borrowed, Returned, Renewed {} record Borrowed(String title, int days) implements Activity {} record Returned(String title) implements Activity {} record Renewed(String title, int extraDays) implements Activity {} // Step 3: add Lost to the permits clause, then uncomment this record. // record Lost(String title, int daysOverdue) implements Activity {} // operation 1: how the activity changes the number of books the member has out static int booksOutDelta(Activity a) { return switch (a) { case Borrowed b -> 1; case Returned r -> -1; case Renewed r -> 0; }; } // operation 2: the line in the member's history static String historyLine(Activity a) { return switch (a) { case Borrowed(var title, var days) -> "borrowed " + title + " for " + days + " days"; case Returned(var title) -> "returned " + title; case Renewed(var title, var extra) -> "renewed " + title + " for " + extra + " more days"; }; } // Step 2: write operation 3 here, sendsReceipt(Activity), as one more switch. public static void main(String[] args) { List<Activity> week = List.of(new Borrowed("Dune", 21), new Borrowed("Emma", 21), new Returned("Dune"), new Renewed("Emma", 14)); int booksOut = 0; for (Activity a : week) { booksOut += booksOutDelta(a); System.out.println(historyLine(a)); } System.out.println("books out: " + booksOut); } }

sections.h: Project Valhalla: forms printed straight onto the page
sections.html:
Records are identity objects, and lesson 1 showed what that means: == compares references, you can lock on a record, and every new makes a separate object. The IdentityDemo shows one more consequence. An array of records is an array of references, each pointing at a separate object on the heap, the memory where Java keeps its objects:

equals: true, ==: false
shelf[0] == shelf[2]: true, shelf[0] == shelf[1]: false

In the paperwork picture, each record is a form in its own envelope, and the array is a list of where the envelopes are. Reading a form means walking to its envelope and opening it. Project Valhalla, a long-running OpenJDK project, wants small forms printed straight onto the page instead, with no envelope. Its first feature lets a class give up identity:

Java
value record Shelf(short floor, short row) {}        // JDK 28 early-access builds, --enable-preview
Kotlin
@JvmInline
value class Isbn(val value: String)                  // Kotlin today: one property, compiled away

The status is often misreported, so here it is precisely. JEP 401, Value Objects (Preview), is the JDK Enhancement Proposal for this feature. Together with JEP 539 (strict field initialization in the JVM), it was integrated into the JDK's main code line on 31 July 2026. JDK 27 had already branched off, so the feature ships in JDK 28, scheduled for 23 March 2027, and early-access builds of JDK 28 have it now. It's a preview: it needs --enable-preview and can still change. JDK 25, 26 and 27 don't have it.

The Valhalla docs define value objects as immutable objects that lack identity, "distinguished solely by the values of their fields". == compares two value objects by their fields, and identity operations such as synchronized fail. Two identical printed lines are interchangeable, and you can't seal an envelope that isn't there. In return, the JVM may store them flat. In JDK 28 that means two optimizations. Flattening stores a value's fields directly inside the field or array element that holds it, with no separate object and no reference. Scalarization lets code compiled by the JIT (the part of the JVM that turns busy code into machine code) keep the fields in registers and skip creating the object at all.

Here the picture breaks: you don't choose what gets printed onto the page, the JVM does, and only small forms qualify. Flattened values are read and written atomically, in one piece, and must allow null, so value objects with 64 bits or more of field data "cannot normally be flattened". By that rule, a record with a long and anything else is already too big. Scalarization only happens once C2, the JIT's optimizing compiler, has compiled the code, and variables of a general type, including those in generic APIs, aren't flattened. Records whose fields add up to less than 64 bits, such as two short fields, gain first.

With the preview on, 28 JDK classes become value classes, among them Integer, Long, Optional, LocalDate, Instant and Duration. Synchronizing on an Integer then throws IdentityException. Null-restricted types, the other thing people expect from Valhalla, are still draft JEPs.

Kotlin's @JvmInline value class is an older, different trick. It holds one property and is erased to that property where the compiler can: javap, the JDK's class-file reader, shows that describeIsbn(Isbn) compiles to describeIsbn-3aCjwxg(java.lang.String), a plain String under a mangled name. It's boxed, that is, wrapped in a real Isbn object, when used as a generic T, an interface or a nullable type; the demo prints in a List, the element is a Isbn. Kotlin's design notes say the annotation leaves room for real Valhalla value classes later. No such mode has shipped, so a Kotlin data class on JDK 28 is still an identity object.

Don't lean on a record's identity. Then value can be a one-word change later.

In practice that means no == between records, no synchronized on them, and no maps keyed on identity.

From labs/, run javap -p modernjava/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/modernjava/l04/demo/IdentityDemoKt.class. What parameter type does describeIsbn take?

code.title: IdentityDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l04.demo; /** Records are identity objects today. Here is what that identity looks like. */ public class IdentityDemo { // one physical copy of a book: its ISBN and its copy number record Copy(String isbn, int number) {} public static void main(String[] args) { Copy a = new Copy("9780441013593", 1); Copy b = new Copy("9780441013593", 1); System.out.println("equals: " + a.equals(b) + ", ==: " + (a == b)); System.out.println("identity hash codes differ: " + (System.identityHashCode(a) != System.identityHashCode(b))); synchronized (a) { System.out.println("synchronized on a record: allowed, because it has an identity"); } // the Integer box cache lets identity leak into == for some values and not others Integer x = 127, y = 127, p = 128, q = 128; System.out.println("Integer 127 == 127: " + (x == y) + ", 128 == 128: " + (p == q)); // an array of records is an array of references to separate heap objects Copy[] shelf = { a, b, a }; System.out.println("shelf[0] == shelf[2]: " + (shelf[0] == shelf[2]) + ", shelf[0] == shelf[1]: " + (shelf[0] == shelf[1])); } }

alt.title: IdentityDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l04.demo // one physical copy of a book: its ISBN and its copy number data class BookCopy(val isbn: String, val number: Int) // Kotlin's value class today: one property, erased to that property wherever the compiler can @JvmInline value class Isbn(val value: String) fun describeIsbn(isbn: Isbn): String = "ISBN ending ${isbn.value.takeLast(4)}" /** Data classes are identity objects today; @JvmInline value classes are a compile-time trick. */ fun main() { val a = BookCopy("9780441013593", 1) val b = BookCopy("9780441013593", 1) println("==: ${a == b}, ===: ${a === b}") synchronized(a) { println("synchronized on a data class: allowed, because it has an identity") } val isbn = Isbn("9780441013593") println(describeIsbn(isbn)) // compiled to a call taking a plain String val asAny: Any = isbn // used as another type: boxed println("as Any, the object is a ${asAny::class.java.simpleName}") val inList = listOf(isbn) // used as a generic T: boxed println("in a List, the element is a ${(inList[0] as Any)::class.java.simpleName}") }

try.expect: equals: true, ==: false, different identity hash codes, a successful synchronized, Integer 127 == 127: true, 128 == 128: false, and shelf[0] == shelf[2]: true, shelf[0] == shelf[1]: false. With a value record, == would compare fields, so a == b and shelf[0] == shelf[1] would be true, and synchronized would be refused. In Kotlin, javap shows describeIsbn-3aCjwxg(java.lang.String): the value class is erased to a String under a mangled name, and the demo shows it boxed back into an Isbn when stored as Any or in a List.

compare.title: One model and one operation in Java and Kotlin

java.title: HoldResult.java
java.html: public record PickupCode(String value) { public PickupCode { if (value == null || !value.matches("[A-Z0-9]{6}")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad pickup code"); } } public sealed interface HoldResult permits Ready, Unavailable, Waitlisted {} public record Ready(PickupCode code, int shelf) implements HoldResult { public Ready { if (shelf < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("hold shelves start at 1"); } } public record Unavailable(Reason reason) implements HoldResult {} public record Waitlisted(Duration expectedWait) implements HoldResult {} static String screenMessage(HoldResult r) { return switch (r) { case Ready(var code, var shelf) -> "Your book is waiting on hold shelf " + shelf + "."; case Unavailable(var reason) when reason == Reason.ACCOUNT_BLOCKED -> "Please ask at the desk."; case Unavailable u -> "This title is not available right now."; case Waitlisted(var wait) -> "You're on the waiting list. Expected wait: " + wait.toDays() + " days."; }; }

kotlin.title: HoldResult.kt
kotlin.html: @JvmInline value class PickupCode(val value: String) { init { require(value.matches(Regex("[A-Z0-9]{6}"))) { "bad pickup code" } } } sealed interface HoldResult { data class Ready(val code: PickupCode, val shelf: Int) : HoldResult { init { require(shelf >= 1) { "hold shelves start at 1" } } } data class Unavailable(val reason: Reason) : HoldResult data class Waitlisted(val expectedWait: Duration) : HoldResult } fun screenMessage(r: HoldResult): String = when (r) { is HoldResult.Ready -> "Your book is waiting on hold shelf ${r.shelf}." is HoldResult.Unavailable if r.reason == Reason.ACCOUNT_BLOCKED -> "Please ask at the desk." is HoldResult.Unavailable -> "This title is not available right now." is HoldResult.Waitlisted -> "You're on the waiting list. Expected wait: ${r.expectedWait.toDays()} days." }

compare.note: The design is identical: a closed set of outcomes, each with only its own fields, constructors that refuse bad values, and an operation written as one exhaustive switch outside the data. Two things differ. Java's switch takes Ready and Unavailable apart in the label, while Kotlin tests the type and reads r.shelf after a smart cast. And PickupCode is a record in Java, a full object with identity, while Kotlin's @JvmInline value class is usually erased to a plain String. With JDK 28's preview, Java could write value record PickupCode(String value) and give up identity at the JVM level, which Kotlin's value class doesn't do today.

worked.title: From the delivery van's report to a closed model

steps.say: A van carries crates of books between the branches, and the van company's system sends a report at each stop. Its docs say: a DELIVERED report has an arrival date, a DELAYED report has a reason, and a DAMAGED report says how many books were damaged. The DTO encodes none of that.
steps.code: public record VanReportDto(String type, String crateId, LocalDate arrivalDate, String delayReason, Integer damagedBooks) {}

alt.html: data class VanReportDto(val type: String?, val crateId: String?, val arrivalDate: LocalDate?, val delayReason: String?, val damagedBooks: Int?)

steps.say: Write one record per row of the van company's docs. Every field is required, so a record can't be half a DELIVERED report.
steps.code: // 1. one record per valid combination public sealed interface VanReport permits Delivered, Delayed, Damaged {} public record Delivered(String crateId, LocalDate arrivalDate) implements VanReport {} public record Delayed(String crateId, String reason) implements VanReport {} public record Damaged(String crateId, int books) implements VanReport { public Damaged { if (books <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("a damage report needs at least one book"); } }

alt.html: // 1. one class per valid combination, with non-null properties sealed interface VanReport { data class Delivered(val crateId: String, val arrivalDate: LocalDate) : VanReport data class Delayed(val crateId: String, val reason: String) : VanReport data class Damaged(val crateId: String, val books: Int) : VanReport { init { require(books > 0) { "a damage report needs at least one book" } } } }

steps.say: Write the edge. It's the only code that looks at the DTO, and it checks that each type carries its own field. A null where the docs promise a value becomes a clear error here, not a NullPointerException three methods later.
steps.code: // 2. the edge: DTO in, model out static VanReport toReport(VanReportDto d) { Objects.requireNonNull(d.crateId(), "crateId"); return switch (d.type()) { case "DELIVERED" -> new Delivered(d.crateId(), Objects.requireNonNull(d.arrivalDate(), "arrivalDate")); case "DELAYED" -> new Delayed(d.crateId(), Objects.requireNonNull(d.delayReason(), "delayReason")); case "DAMAGED" -> new Damaged(d.crateId(), Objects.requireNonNull(d.damagedBooks(), "damagedBooks")); case null, default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown van report: " + d.type()); }; }

alt.html: // 2. the edge: DTO in, model out fun toReport(d: VanReportDto): VanReport { val id = requireNotNull(d.crateId) { "crateId" } return when (d.type) { "DELIVERED" -> VanReport.Delivered(id, requireNotNull(d.arrivalDate) { "arrivalDate" }) "DELAYED" -> VanReport.Delayed(id, requireNotNull(d.delayReason) { "delayReason" }) "DAMAGED" -> VanReport.Damaged(id, requireNotNull(d.damagedBooks) { "damagedBooks" }) else -> throw IllegalArgumentException("unknown van report: ${d.type}") } }

steps.say: Now the code that acts on a report. The old version was thirty lines of if ("DELIVERED".equals(type) && arrivalDate != null). The new one is a switch with no default, so a new kind of report from the van company shows up as a compile error, not as a report that is silently ignored.
steps.code: // 3. behind the edge: trust the types static void apply(VanReport r, Catalogue catalogue) { switch (r) { case Delivered(var id, var date) -> catalogue.markArrived(id, date); case Delayed(var id, var reason) -> catalogue.tellBranch(id, reason); case Damaged(var id, int books) -> catalogue.orderReplacements(id, books); } }

alt.html: // 3. behind the edge: trust the types fun apply(r: VanReport, catalogue: Catalogue) = when (r) { is VanReport.Delivered -> catalogue.markArrived(r.crateId, r.arrivalDate) is VanReport.Delayed -> catalogue.tellBranch(r.crateId, r.reason) is VanReport.Damaged -> catalogue.orderReplacements(r.crateId, r.books) }

lab.title: Parse a catalogue reply into a model with no illegal states
steps: Run the tests: all ten fail. This lab is in Kotlin. The model is in HoldModel.kt, and the edge and the operation are in HoldReplies.kt.
Make the model refuse what can't be real: write the init checks in PickupCode, Ready and Waitlisted (TODO 1 to 3). Three tests should pass now.
Write parse (TODO 4) as one when on the status. Let the constructors do their own checks, and turn their IllegalArgumentException into Rejected.
Write screenMessage (TODO 5) as one when with guards and no else.
When all ten pass, add data class Transferring(val fromBranch: String) : HoldResult to the model and run ./gradlew :modernjava:compileKotlin. Which function does kotlinc point at? Remove it again.
hints: A value class may have an init block: init { require(Regex("[A-Z0-9]{6}").matches(value)) { "bad pickup code: $value" } }.
Duration is Comparable, so expectedWait >= Duration.ofDays(1) && expectedWait <= Duration.ofDays(365) works in Kotlin.
Wrap the whole when in try { ... } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { Rejected(e.message ?: "invalid reply") }. Duration.ofDays(0) is fine; it's Waitlisted that refuses it.
After a branch like raw.pickupCode == null -> Rejected(...), Kotlin smart-casts raw.pickupCode to String in the later branches, because it's a val of a class in the same module.
A guard looks like is Unavailable if result.reason == Reason.ACCOUNT_BLOCKED -> ....

drill.title: Model a reply from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. A renewal reply has a type ("GRANTED", "REFUSED" or "QUEUED"), a loanId, and a refusalCode that is present only when the renewal was refused. Write the sealed model in Java so that a refusal can't lack its code, and a parse(type, loanId, refusalCode) that throws IllegalArgumentException for an unknown or missing type. Then write the Kotlin version.

answer.html: sealed interface RenewalReply permits Granted, Refused, Queued {} record Granted(String loanId) implements RenewalReply {} record Refused(String loanId, String refusalCode) implements RenewalReply { Refused { Objects.requireNonNull(refusalCode, "refusalCode"); } // a refusal always has a code } record Queued(String loanId) implements RenewalReply {} static RenewalReply parse(String type, String loanId, String refusalCode) { return switch (type) { case "GRANTED" -> new Granted(loanId); case "REFUSED" -> new Refused(loanId, refusalCode); case "QUEUED" -> new Queued(loanId); case null, default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown renewal reply: " + type); }; }

alt.html: sealed interface RenewalReply { data class Granted(val loanId: String) : RenewalReply data class Refused(val loanId: String, val refusalCode: String) : RenewalReply // non-null: always has a code data class Queued(val loanId: String) : RenewalReply } fun parse(type: String?, loanId: String, refusalCode: String?): RenewalReply = when (type) { "GRANTED" -> RenewalReply.Granted(loanId) "REFUSED" -> RenewalReply.Refused(loanId, requireNotNull(refusalCode) { "refusalCode" }) "QUEUED" -> RenewalReply.Queued(loanId) else -> throw IllegalArgumentException("unknown renewal reply: $type") }

recap: Model each valid combination as its own record under a sealed interface, and check values in the constructors. A shape that can't be written down can't reach your code.
Records are product types (this and that) and sealed interfaces are sum types (this or that). Most messages are a few alternatives, each a fixed set of fields.
Parse untrusted input into the model once, at the edge, and return a result instead of throwing. Behind the edge, trust the types.

Write the rules as functions that switch over the data. A new operation is one function; a new type breaks every switch, and the compiler lists them. Keep interfaces with methods for hierarchies others extend.
Valhalla's value objects are a preview in JDK 28 (early-access builds now, release scheduled for March 2027), not in JDK 25, 26 or 27. Records are identity objects, so don't depend on their identity.
The limit: the model is only as good as its edge. Data that skips parse, or a nullable status field sneaked back into the records, brings the 48 shapes back.

explain.prompt: Your team lead asks: "Should we move the library's data to records and sealed types now, or wait for Valhalla to make it fast?" Answer in your own words: what the data-oriented style gives you today, where you would and wouldn't use it, and what Valhalla changes.
explain.answer: The data-oriented style pays off today, with no new JDK: records and sealed types are standard since JDK 17, and pattern switches since 21. Modeling each valid outcome as its own record means contradictory states can't be built, parsing at the edge means only valid values get in, and exhaustive switches mean the compiler tells us every place to update when a type is added. I'd use it for closed data such as hold results, desk events and copy statuses, and keep ordinary interfaces for things others extend, like the partner libraries' items. Valhalla changes performance and identity; it doesn't change this design. JEP 401 is only a preview in JDK 28, and even there, a record with a long and anything else wouldn't normally be flattened. So we shouldn't wait for it; we should just avoid depending on record identity, so that adding value later is easy.

deeper.html:
Brian Goetz's January 2026 design note, "Data-Oriented Programming for Java: Beyond Records", says where Project Amber, the OpenJDK project behind records and patterns, goes next. It calls records, sealed classes and record patterns "the first feature arc of 'data-oriented programming' for Java", and announces the next arc: carrier classes and carrier interfaces. A carrier class is a normal class with a record-style state description in its header. It would declare its own fields and need not be final, yet still have a canonical constructor, accessors and a deconstruction pattern. So data that is almost a record (one cached field, one derived value) wouldn't force you back to writing everything by hand.

The note also describes reconstruction, the with expression from JEP 468, and points out how much its block resembles a compact constructor body: the component variables start with the old values, your block changes some of them, and the canonical constructor builds the new value, so the checks still run. Goetz explains that JEP 468 has been "on hold" until there was a path to extend it beyond records. The note also mentions an upcoming pattern assignment statement, for taking a record apart in an ordinary assignment.

None of this is in a JDK or a JEP you can use. The design direction is useful anyway: it says the language will keep making "model the data with records and sealed types, switch over it" cheaper, so code written in that style today is code the platform is moving toward.

On the Valhalla side, the next pieces on the project page are null-restricted storage, array improvements, unifying primitives with classes, and a JVM that can specialize generic code for each type it's used with. Only the first piece, value objects, has a JEP that has been integrated, and it's a preview.
